title: Public Restrooms and Bidet Toilets in Korea: A Beginner's Guide
html:
Public restrooms are one of those small things nobody warns you about before a trip — and then you land in Korea and suddenly there's a control panel next to the toilet with a dozen Korean buttons. Don't worry. Korean restrooms are actually some of the cleanest and most convenient in the world once you know what you're looking at. Here's everything a first-time visitor needs to know: where to find a restroom, how the famous bidet toilet works, what to do if you hit an old-style squat toilet, and the flush-or-bin toilet paper question.

Finding a Restroom Is Never Hard in Korea

A restroom is called a hwajangsil (화장실) in Korean, and you'll see the word — or the universal little person icons — signposted almost everywhere. Every subway station in Korea has a free public restroom, usually near the ticket gates. Department stores, large bookstores, museums, palaces, and highway rest stops all have clean, free restrooms open to anyone, not just paying customers. Unlike some countries in Europe, you will basically never be asked to pay to use one.

If you're out on the street and can't spot one, open Naver Map or Kakao Map (the two apps most people use to get around Korea) and search "화장실" or "toilet" — public restrooms are marked on both, including ones tucked inside parks or shopping arcades that are easy to miss otherwise.

A free public restroom building at Seoul Grand Park — this kind of clean, clearly marked facility is typical across Korea's parks and public spaces. Source: Wikimedia Commons (photographer/license to be confirmed — see note below).

Meet the Bidet Toilet: Korea's High-Tech Standard

Most hotels, cafés, malls, and subway station restrooms in Korea have an electronic bidet toilet seat — a normal-looking toilet with a small control panel built into the seat or mounted on the wall beside it. It can wash and dry you with warm water instead of (or in addition to) toilet paper, and usually heats the seat too, which is a nice surprise in winter.

The buttons are almost always labeled in Korean only, which trips up a lot of first-timers. The good news: you never have to use them. The toilet works completely normally with regular toilet paper if you just ignore the panel. If you do want to try it, look for a button showing a small icon of a person with water lines near their backside (rear wash) or near the front (for women, a separate front wash). Before pressing anything else, find the STOP button first — it's usually the biggest or reddest one — so you can shut the water off quickly if it turns on unexpectedly. One more thing: the panel usually isn't the flush. The actual flush is often a separate small lever or button on the toilet tank or the side wall, so don't stand there pressing bidet buttons hoping one of them flushes.

An electronic bidet toilet seat (this one a Woongjin "LooLoo" model) — Korean bathrooms often have a similar panel with buttons for rear wash, front wash, water pressure, and seat heating. Source: Wikimedia Commons (photographer/license to be confirmed — see note below).

What locals actually do: most Koreans barely touch the wash buttons daily and mainly use the heated seat function in winter — so don't feel like you're missing some essential ritual if you skip the panel entirely.

Squat Toilets: The Older-Style Option You Might Still Encounter

Squat toilets (called jaeraeshik hwajangsil, 재래식 화장실, meaning "traditional-style restroom") are much less common than they used to be, but you'll still run into one occasionally — sometimes as just one stall out of several in a subway station, or in older buildings, traditional markets, temples, and restrooms along hiking trails. Instead of a raised bowl, it's a porcelain trough set into the floor with a curved hood at one end.

To use one: stand over it facing the raised hood (that's usually the end closer to the door, and often where the flush handle is), with one foot on each side, then squat down. Roll up long pants or a skirt so nothing drags on the floor, and keep your bag on the door hook if there is one rather than the ground. It feels awkward the first time, but it's over quickly — and most public buildings now offer at least one regular seated toilet alongside it, so you can usually just wait for the next stall if you'd rather not.

An older-style squat toilet still found in some older buildings in Korea. Source: Wikimedia Commons (photographer/license to be confirmed — see note below).

Toilet Paper, Trash Bins, and Reading the Signs

This is the part that confuses almost every first-time visitor. For years, the standard advice was "never flush toilet paper in Korea, always use the bin." That's changed a lot: since a 2018 nationwide rule, most public restrooms removed the trash bin from inside each stall entirely (any small bin you do see is almost always for sanitary products only, not general toilet paper). In modern buildings — hotels, cafés, malls, newer subway stations — the plumbing is built to handle paper, so you can flush it like at home.

The exception is older buildings with older pipes, where flushing paper can genuinely clog the system. The easiest rule for a traveler: look for a sign or pictogram near the toilet. If there's a bin and a sign asking you to use it, follow that. If you see nothing unusual, flushing is almost always fine. You don't need to read Korean — these signs are almost always pictures.

One more quirk worth knowing: in some older public restrooms (highway rest stops, some subway stations), the toilet paper roll is a large shared dispenser outside the stalls, near the sinks or entrance — not inside each individual stall. Grab what you need on your way in, just in case.

A standard restroom stall in Korea — free to use, and almost always cleaner than travelers expect. Source: Wikimedia Commons (photographer/license to be confirmed — see note below).

What locals actually do: most Koreans carry a small pack of tissues in their bag anyway, just in case a dispenser is empty or a restroom is one of the more basic older ones — it's an easy habit to copy for your trip.

Quick reference — what you'll find and what to do:

Toilet typeWhere you'll typically see itWhat to do
Electronic bidet seatHotels, cafés, malls, newer subway stationsIgnore the buttons if unsure — it works like a normal toilet with paper
Standard seated toiletHomes, older buildings, some public restroomsUse like any Western toilet; check for a bin/sign about paper
Squat toiletOccasional stall in older buildings, hiking trails, marketsFace the raised hood, straddle the footpads, squat down

💬 Had a funny (or confusing) bathroom moment in Korea, or still not sure how something works? Ask away in the comments — happy to help!
meta_description: A beginner's guide to Korean public restrooms: how to use the electronic bidet toilet, handle squat toilets, and know when to flush or bin toilet paper.
